questions.stem: The total wave function of a system of identical fermions must be:

options.C: symmetric under exchange of any two particles
options.D: antisymmetric under exchange of any two particles

explanation.whyCorrect: Spin-statistics: half-integer spin particles have totally antisymmetric wave functions; integer-spin particles have symmetric ones.

whyWrong.A: Exchange symmetry is fixed by spin, not by the Hamiltonian.
whyWrong.B: Reality is irrelevant to exchange symmetry.

explanation.howToModify: Ask what happens to an antisymmetric wave function when two particles share all coordinates (it vanishes).

questions.stem: The Pauli exclusion principle follows from:

options.A: antisymmetry of the many-fermion wave function

explanation.whyCorrect: An antisymmetric product (Slater determinant) with two identical single-particle states has two equal rows/columns and vanishes.

whyWrong.B: Uncertainty does not forbid double occupancy.
whyWrong.D: Pauli exclusion holds even for non-interacting fermions (e.g. neutrons in a star).

explanation.howToModify: Ask why neutron stars resist collapse (neutron degeneracy pressure).
explanation.howToAvoid: Exclusion is a symmetry effect, not a force.

questions.stem: Two non-interacting identical spin-\(\tfrac12\) fermions in the same spin state are placed in a 1D infinite well with single-particle levels \(E_n = n^2E_1\). The ground-state energy of the pair is:

explanation.whyCorrect: Same spin state ⇒ spatial part antisymmetric ⇒ they must occupy different levels: \(E_1 + E_2 = E_1 + 4E_1 = 5E_1\).

whyWrong.A: Correct for bosons or for opposite spins (singlet).
whyWrong.D: Both in \(n=2\): forbidden and not minimal.

explanation.howToModify: Ask for the answer when the spins form a singlet (\(2E_1\)).
explanation.howToAvoid: Read the spin condition: same spin state → different orbitals.

questions.stem: Compared with distinguishable particles, identical particles in a spatially symmetric state tend to be:

options.A: unable to occupy the same region

explanation.whyCorrect: \(\langle (x_1-x_2)^2\rangle_\pm = \langle(x_1-x_2)^2\rangle_d \mp 2|\langle x\rangle_{ab}|^2\): symmetric states bunch together ('exchange attraction'), antisymmetric states anti-bunch.

whyWrong.A: Describes antisymmetric states at coincident points.
whyWrong.B: This applies to antisymmetric spatial states.

explanation.trapUsed: Swapping the bunching and anti-bunching cases.
explanation.howToModify: Ask how this explains the covalent bond (symmetric spatial, spin singlet).

questions.stem: In the ground state of helium (both electrons in \(1s\)), the spin state of the two electrons is:

options.A: an equal mixture of singlet and triplet

explanation.whyCorrect: Both electrons in the symmetric spatial state \(1s(1)1s(2)\); total antisymmetry requires the antisymmetric spin singlet. Hence ground-state helium is para-helium.

whyWrong.A: Total spin is a good quantum number here; no mixing.
whyWrong.C: A triplet would require an antisymmetric spatial part, impossible with both in \(1s\).

explanation.howToModify: Ask why the lowest ortho-helium state is \(1s2s\,^3S\).
explanation.howToAvoid: Spatially symmetric ⇒ spin antisymmetric (singlet) for fermions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a boson?

explanation.whyCorrect: \(^4\)He has 2 protons, 2 neutrons, 2 electrons — an even number of fermions — so its total spin is an integer and it obeys Bose statistics.
explanation.howToModify: Ask which isotope of helium becomes superfluid at 2.17 K (\(^4\)He).
